New to C#? Start here

{{dynamic_1}}

C# is the language you write. .NET provides tools and ready-made features that run your program. Visual Studio is the app where you edit, build and run it.

Start with C# foundations. Then follow the web learning order: 1. Understand web apps, 2. Try beginner CRUD, 3. Organise code with controllers, then 4. Save data in a database. You can return to the other units whenever you need them.

  1. Read the short explanation first. You do not need to memorise every word.
  2. Download the example ZIP, extract it, then open its .csproj file in Visual Studio. This file tells Visual Studio how to build the project.
  3. Wait for package restore. A package is a library of ready-made code. NuGet downloads the packages listed in the project.
  4. Follow one numbered part at a time. Add the parts to the same named file, in order. The full version is below if you get stuck.
  5. Choose Build > Build Solution to check the code. Then follow this lesson's run instructions and compare the result with its expected output.
  6. Change one small thing, run again and explain what changed. Try the task before reading its answer.
Try your first C# program in a separate Console App

In Visual Studio choose Create a new project > Console App (C#), then select .NET 10. Replace everything in Program.cs with this code. Keep this practice project separate from the API and desktop projects. 

// Store a name as text.
string name = "Lefa";
// Store an age as a whole number.
int age = 22;
// Print a message. Braces insert the stored values.
Console.WriteLine($"Hello {name}. You are {age}.");

Choose Debug > Start Without Debugging. Expected output: Hello Lefa. You are 22.

string means text. int means a whole number. A variable is a named place to store a value. = stores the value on the right in the variable on the left. Double quotes surround text. A semicolon ends these statements. // starts a comment for the reader; the program ignores it.

Try it: change the name to your own and add 1 to the age. Predict the message, then run it again.

Simple meanings of words used in these lessons
Class and object
A class describes a kind of thing. An object is one thing created from that description. A Student class can describe many student objects.
Property
A named value on an object, such as a student's Name or Age.
Method, parameter and return
A method is a named set of steps. A parameter receives input. Return sends a result back to the code that called it.
List and LINQ
A list holds several items. LINQ lets you find, sort or select information from those items.
API, request and response
An API lets programs ask each other to do work. A request is the question sent to it. A response is the result sent back.
Route and endpoint
A route is an address pattern such as /api/students. An endpoint connects an address and HTTP action to the code that handles it.
CRUD
Create adds an item. Read shows it. Update changes it. Delete removes it.
DTO and JSON
A DTO is a small object used to carry data into or out of an API. JSON is a text format used to send that data.
Database, EF Core and migration
A database stores rows that remain after the app closes. EF Core helps C# work with those rows. A migration describes a change to database tables.
Service and dependency injection
A service does a job for other code. Dependency injection means .NET supplies a registered service when your code needs it.
async and await
Some work, such as reading a database, takes time. Await lets a method wait for that work without keeping its thread busy. Async allows await in the method. It does not automatically create a new thread.
Build error and runtime error
A build error stops the code from compiling. A runtime error happens after the program starts. Read the first error, check its file and line, then fix one issue at a time.
